plan.topic: Plague in the US: where it still occurs naturally (the rural West), how people catch it (flea bites, handling infected animals, sick pets), and practical prevention for hikers, campers and pet owners, all from CDC primary sources
plan.angle: A calm, evergreen explainer built only from CDC primary pages (Plague home, Maps and Statistics, Prevention, Plague and pets) with their live 'last reviewed' dates. In the first 15 s: plague still turns up in the US, it's rare, and it's treatable with antibiotics, especially when started early (CDC). Copy the case figure word for word from CDC's Maps and Statistics page at publish time (on 10-09 it read 'an average of five human plague cases are reported each year', range 0–17). Never use 7, and keep 'human' and 'average'. Chapters: (1) what Yersinia pestis is and how it lives in wild rodents and their fleas; (2) where US human cases cluster, using only the regions CDC names; (3) how people are infected, using CDC's own routes (flea bites, handling infected animals, infected pets, especially cats), with human cases kept separate from animal or flea findings; (4) which form most US cases are, in CDC's own words, plus one scoped line that pneumonic plague is the form that can spread between people through close contact, and CDC's calming fact that there's been no person-to-person spread in the US since 1924 (only if the live page says so); (5) prevention from CDC: don't touch sick or dead rodents, use insect repellent, reduce rodent habitat around the home, keep pets' flea control up to date, with the caveat that dog flea products can be toxic to cats, and keep pets from roaming and hunting; (6) if your pet gets sick, see a vet; (7) symptoms after possible exposure (fever, chills, swollen painful lymph nodes for bubonic; CDC's pneumonic signs in full: fever, cough, shortness of breath, chest pain), then 'contact a doctor or local health authority urgently and mention where you've been'. No self-treatment or antibiotic stockpiling. Leave out the Irkutsk status and anything credited to Russian bodies or WHO. If a hook is used, one line says the US situation is separate, with nothing attributed. No 'near you' phrasing and no rats-as-horror visuals. Close with 'If you're worried, talk to a health professional.' Description: plain text, 1,500 characters or fewer, up to 4 CDC sources with full canonical URLs, and a complete last line.
plan.working_title: Plague in the US: Where It Still Occurs and How Hikers and Pet Owners Stay Safe (CDC)
plan.why: Our best-performing plague format (place + agency + prevention; 67 YouTube views, 107 Instagram reach, first shares). It's rising on the radar (momentum 80) and it's evergreen, built only from stable CDC pages, so it's easy to verify with no fast-moving news claims. It doesn't overlap S1–S3, C1 or the dropped lab-safety video.

package.description:
Plague in the US is rare: CDC says an average of five human plague cases are reported each year (range 0-17; CDC page checked Oct 10, 2026), mostly in the rural West.
CDC says plague bacteria are most often transmitted by the bite of an infected flea, and people can also be infected by handling infected animals or, rarely, by sick cats.
CDC says plague can be cured with antibiotics, but they must be given promptly.

If fever, chills or painful swollen lymph nodes, or fever, cough, shortness of breath and chest pain, appear after a possible exposure, contact a doctor or local health authority urgently and say where you've been. Don't treat yourself or stockpile antibiotics. FDA: if a flea product is made for dogs, don't use it on cats. Ask your vet.

This video is for general education, not medical advice. If you're worried, talk to a health professional.

Sources:
CDC, Plague Maps and Statistics: https://www.cdc.gov/plague/maps-statistics/index.html
CDC, How Plague Spreads: https://www.cdc.gov/plague/causes/index.html
CDC, Preventing Plague: https://www.cdc.gov/plague/prevention/index.html
FDA, Safe Use of Flea and Tick Products in Pets: https://www.fda.gov/consumers/consumer-updates/safe-use-flea-and-tick-products-pets

script.working_title: Plague in the US: Where It Still Occurs and How Hikers and Pet Owners Stay Safe (CDC)
script.hook_pattern: Counterintuitive claim plus stakes and specificity. The opening says plague still turns up in the US and gives CDC's exact wording on the average number of human cases a year. Within the first 15 seconds it also says the disease is rare and curable with prompt antibiotics. One unattributed line says the US situation is separate from the news, as the brief requires. Following the brief, the Irkutsk status and anything credited to Russian bodies or WHO were removed. An open loop (the moment on a trail 'when the animals vanish') pays off in 'Staying safe outdoors'. A second loop (the year 1924) pays off in 'Which form, and 1924'.

scenes.narration: Plague still turns up in the United States. Not in a history book. In real people, most years.
CDC's page puts it this way: an average of five human plague cases are reported each year, with a range of 0 to 17.

visual.stat_label: Average US human plague cases a year (CDC)
visual.stock_query: calm US map with small dots

scenes.narration: So it's rare. And CDC says plague can be cured with antibiotics, but they must be given promptly.
You may have seen plague in the news lately. The US situation is separate, and it's what this video is about.
scenes.retention_device: Context reset that frames the video

scenes.narration: In the next few minutes, you'll learn where US cases cluster, how people actually catch it, and the simple habits that protect hikers, campers and pet owners.

visual.stock_query: checklist with hiking boots and cat

scenes.retention_device: Clear promise of what the viewer gets

scenes.narration: And stick around, because CDC warns about one situation outdoors where the risk goes up. It's not when you see an animal. It's when the animals have suddenly died off.
scenes.retention_device: Main open loop, paid off in 'Staying safe outdoors'

scenes.narration: First, what plague actually is.
Plague is caused by a bacterium called Yersinia pestis. Think of it less like a visitor and more like a long-term resident of the wild.
scenes.retention_device: Analogy that makes the biology stick

scenes.narration: CDC explains that the bacteria cycle between wild rodents and their fleas. A flea bites an infected rodent, picks up the bacteria, then bites the next animal.

visual.stock_query: looping arrow between squirrel and flea

scenes.retention_device: Simple mechanism, shown as a loop

scenes.narration: In the western US, CDC lists animals you'd recognise among those that can be affected by plague: rock squirrels, wood rats, ground squirrels, prairie dogs and chipmunks.

visual.stock_query: friendly cartoon prairie dog and chipmunk

scenes.retention_device: Surprise: the cute animals you already know

scenes.narration: People only get involved when they cross into that cycle. And that crossing is what the rest of this video is about.
scenes.retention_device: Sets up the 'how people catch it' chapter

scenes.narration: But how did a disease known for medieval Europe end up in the hills of New Mexico? That story starts on a ship.
CDC says plague was first introduced into the United States in 1900, by rat-infested steamships that had sailed from affected areas.

visual.stat_label: Plague first introduced into the US (CDC)

scenes.narration: Epidemics hit port cities. The last urban plague epidemic in the US was in Los Angeles, from 1924 through 1925.
scenes.retention_device: Specific date that sets up a later payoff

scenes.narration: Then something changed. Plague spread from city rats to rural rodent species, and became entrenched in many areas of the western US.
scenes.on_screen_text: From cities to the rural West

visual.stock_query: arrow from city to western hills

scenes.narration: Since then, CDC says, plague has occurred as scattered cases in rural areas. Hold on to that year, 1924. It comes back later, with some good news.
scenes.retention_device: Second open loop, paid off in 'Which form, and 1924'

scenes.narration: So where exactly do these cases happen?
CDC names two regions where most US human cases occur.
The first: northern New Mexico, northern Arizona and southern Colorado.
The second: California, southern Oregon and far western Nevada.
Notice the pattern. US plague is a story of the rural West, of open land where wild rodents and their fleas live.
And remember the scale. An average of 5 human cases a year, across the whole country.

visual.stat_label: Average human cases a year, whole US (CDC)
visual.stock_query: whole US map with few dots

scenes.narration: So this isn't a reason to cancel your camping trip. It's a reason to know a few habits, the same way you'd know about ticks or sunburn.
scenes.on_screen_text: Know the habits, keep the trip

scenes.narration: Here's the question that matters most: how does a person actually end up infected?
scenes.retention_device: Cliffhanger question before the section change

scenes.narration: CDC describes a few main routes.
Route one, and the most common: flea bites. CDC says plague bacteria are most often transmitted by the bite of an infected flea.
That's a flea that has fed on an infected rodent. When it bites a person, it can pass the bacteria on.

visual.stock_query: flea jumping from squirrel to boot

scenes.retention_device: Ties back to the rodent-flea loop

scenes.narration: Route two: handling an infected animal. CDC says people can become infected when handling tissue or body fluids of a plague-infected animal.
CDC's own example is a hunter skinning a rabbit or other infected animal without proper precautions.

visual.stock_query: hunter in forest putting on gloves

scenes.narration: Route three is the one most people don't expect: pets. And CDC singles out one pet in particular.

visual.stock_query: dog and cat silhouettes behind curtain

scenes.narration: Cats. CDC says cats are particularly susceptible to plague, and can be infected by eating infected rodents.
scenes.retention_device: Immediate payoff of the mini loop

scenes.narration: A sick cat can pass infectious droplets to its owner or to a veterinarian. CDC says there continue to be rare cases of pneumonic plague among people exposed to sick cats.
Dogs matter too, as a possible taxi for fleas. CDC says pets that roam freely are more likely to come in contact with infected animals or fleas, and could bring them into the home.
One important distinction. When you hear that plague was found in a prairie dog colony or in fleas, that's an animal finding, not a human case.

visual.myth: Plague found in animals means people are sick
visual.fact: Animal or flea findings are not human cases
visual.stock_query: prairie dog colony with info sign

scenes.narration: Think of those findings as a cue to be extra careful in that area, not as a count of sick people.
Plague comes in three forms, and which one you're talking about changes everything.
Bubonic plague affects the lymph nodes. Septicemic plague is in the bloodstream. Pneumonic plague is in the lungs.
So which form do most Americans get? CDC's answer: over 80% of United States plague cases have been the bubonic form.

visual.stat_label: US plague cases that were bubonic (CDC)

scenes.narration: Here's why that's reassuring. According to CDC, the only way plague spreads between people is through respiratory droplets from someone with pneumonic plague.

visual.stock_query: two people at distance, droplet icons

scenes.narration: And CDC says that kind of spread requires direct and close contact with the person or animal with pneumonic plague.
And now, the payoff on 1924.
Remember 1924? CDC says person-to-person spread of plague has not been documented in the United States since 1924.
That's more than a century without documented person-to-person spread in the US.
scenes.retention_device: Reframes the stat in plain terms

scenes.narration: But there's a catch. CDC says pneumonic plague can also develop from untreated bubonic or septicemic plague, after the bacteria spread to the lungs.

visual.stock_query: arrow from lymph node to lungs

scenes.narration: Which is exactly why early treatment matters so much. We'll get to the warning signs. First, how to stop it getting that far.
Let's start outdoors: hikers, campers, hunters and anyone who works on open land.
Now, the payoff from the start. CDC warns about places where rodents have recently died from plague.
scenes.retention_device: Payoff of the main open loop

scenes.narration: During a plague outbreak in animals, many rodents die, and their hungry fleas look for other sources of blood. People and animals visiting those places are at risk from flea bites.
So a prairie dog town that's suddenly gone quiet, especially with dead animals around? That's your cue to keep your distance, and to report dead animals to your local health department.
Rule one: leave sick or dead animals alone. If you have questions about a dead animal, CDC says to contact your local health department.
scenes.on_screen_text: Leave sick or dead animals alone

scenes.narration: If you hunt or need to handle a potentially infected animal, CDC recommends wearing gloves.
Rule two: CDC says use repellent if you think you could be exposed to fleas during activities like camping, hiking or working outdoors.
CDC says products with DEET can go on skin and clothing, and products with permethrin go on clothing only. Always follow the label.
Rule three is about your home, especially if you live near open land in these regions.
CDC advises reducing rodent habitat around your home, work and recreation areas. That means clearing brush, rock piles, junk and cluttered firewood.
And remove possible rodent food, like pet food and wild animal food left outside. No buffet means fewer rodents, and fewer fleas.
Quick question for you: where does your pet sleep at night? Keep that answer in mind.
scenes.retention_device: Direct question to the viewer before the section change

scenes.narration: Because for pet owners, a few habits do a lot of the work.

visual.stock_query: happy dog and cat title card

scenes.narration: First, keep fleas off your pets with flea control products, and keep them up to date. Your vet can help you pick the right one.
One crucial caveat: the FDA says if a flea product is made for dogs, don't use it on cats. Ask your vet which product is right for your pet.
scenes.on_screen_text: Dog flea products: not for cats

visual.myth: Any flea product is fine for any pet
visual.fact: FDA: don't use dog flea products on cats
visual.stock_query: dog product box crossed near cat

scenes.retention_device: Safety warning most viewers don't know

scenes.narration: Second, CDC advises not letting pets roam freely in plague areas. Animals that roam freely are more likely to come in contact with plague-infected animals or fleas, and could bring them into homes.
Third, the bed. CDC advises not letting dogs or cats that roam free in areas where plague occurs sleep on your bed.

visual.stock_query: dog sleeping in its own bed

scenes.retention_device: Payoff of the 'where does your pet sleep' question

scenes.narration: And if your pet gets sick, CDC's advice is simple: seek care from a veterinarian as soon as possible.

visual.stock_query: owner carrying cat into vet clinic

scenes.narration: Tell the vet where your pet has been, so they can think about plague and protect themselves and you.
scenes.on_screen_text: Tell the vet where it's been

visual.stock_query: owner talking to vet at counter

scenes.retention_device: Sets up the same move for humans

scenes.narration: Now the part that can genuinely save a life: knowing the warning signs after a possible exposure.
scenes.retention_device: Payoff of the 'warning signs' loop, with high stakes

scenes.narration: For bubonic plague, CDC lists fever, headache, chills and weakness, plus one or more swollen, painful lymph nodes, called buboes.
CDC explains that the bacteria multiply in a lymph node near where they entered the body.

visual.stock_query: simple body outline lymph node glow

scenes.narration: Septicemic plague can cause fever, chills, extreme weakness and abdominal pain. CDC says it can be the first sign of plague, or develop from untreated bubonic plague.
For pneumonic plague, CDC's list includes fever, headache, weakness, cough, shortness of breath and chest pain, with a pneumonia that develops quickly.
On their own, symptoms like fever usually mean something far more common. What changes the picture is a possible exposure.
So if these symptoms appear after time in a plague area, especially after flea bites, handling a wild animal or contact with a sick pet, contact a doctor or local health authority urgently.
And mention where you've been. That one sentence helps your clinician think of plague and test for it quickly.

visual.stock_query: patient talking to doctor with map

scenes.narration: CDC says plague can be cured with antibiotics, but they must be given promptly to prevent serious illness or death.
What you should not do is treat yourself. No leftover pills, and no stockpiling antibiotics. Diagnosis and treatment belong with a doctor.

visual.myth: Leftover antibiotics at home will do
visual.fact: Diagnosis and treatment belong with a doctor

scenes.narration: Let's pull it all together.
Plague still occurs in the US: an average of 5 human cases a year, according to CDC, mostly in the rural West.

visual.stat_label: Average US human cases a year (CDC)

scenes.narration: Outdoors: leave sick or dead animals alone, use repellent, and keep away from places where rodents have suddenly died off.

items: Hands off sick or dead animals

scenes.narration: At home: clear brush, rock piles, clutter and outdoor food that attract rodents.
For pets: keep flea control current, ask your vet for cat-safe products, don't let pets roam, and see a vet if they get sick.
For you: fever, chills or painful swollen lymph nodes, or fever, cough, shortness of breath and chest pain after a possible exposure means contact a doctor or local health authority urgently.

items: Fever, cough, shortness of breath, chest pain

scenes.narration: Rare, treatable, and a few simple habits lower your risk even more. That's the real picture of plague in the US today.
If you want calm, clear health explainers like this, subscribe. Next, we break down pneumonic plague symptoms and exactly when to get urgent care.

factcheck.summary:
I checked every CDC and FDA claim against the live pages on 2026-10-10, and all of them hold up.

**What matches the sources:**
- **CDC Maps & Statistics (updated and reviewed Oct 7, 2026):**
  - "An average of five human plague cases are reported each year", with a range of 0–17.
  - Plague arrived in 1900 on rat-infested steamships.
  - The last urban epidemic was in Los Angeles, 1924–1925.
  - It then spread from city rats to rural rodents in the western US, and now occurs as scattered rural cases.
  - The two regions are worded exactly as CDC words them.
  - "Over 80%" of US cases have been bubonic.
- **How Plague Spreads:**
  - Flea bites are the most common route.
  - The animal list matches, and the hunter-skinning-a-rabbit example is CDC's own.
  - CDC says cats are particularly susceptible and can catch plague by eating infected rodents.
  - CDC notes rare pneumonic cases in people exposed to sick cats.
  - Person-to-person spread happens only through pneumonic droplets, requires direct and close contact, and has not been documented in the US since 1924.
  - CDC describes rodent die-offs that send hungry fleas looking for new hosts.
- **Preventing Plague (Mar 5, 2025):**
  - Remove rodent habitat and food sources.
  - Wear gloves to handle animals.
  - Use repellent: DEET on skin and clothing, permethrin on clothing only.
  - Use flea control on pets, and don't let them roam.
  - Don't let free-roaming pets sleep on your bed.
  - See a vet as soon as possible if a pet gets sick.
  - Contact the local health department with questions about dead animals.
  - The roaming-pets sentence is quoted word for word.
- **Signs & Symptoms:** the symptom lists for bubonic, septicemic and pneumonic plague all match, including cough and chest pain for pneumonic. So do the lymph-node explanation and how the forms progress.
- **About Plague (Aug 24, 2026):** "can be cured with antibiotics, but these must be given promptly to prevent serious illness or death".
- **FDA (2021):** "If the product is for use on dogs, don't use it on cats."

**Safety and framing:**
- The script tells viewers to "contact a doctor or local health authority urgently" and ties the symptoms to a possible exposure.
- It warns against self-treatment and stockpiling antibiotics.
- It includes the cat-safety caveat and ends with "If you're worried, talk to a health professional."
- There is no fear-bait.
- No Irkutsk status lines remain, which is what the brief asked for.
- The title is 86 characters, starts with "Plague" and keeps "(CDC)".

**Polish points (all minor):**
- The "animals vanish" hook goes a bit beyond CDC's "rodents have recently died" wording.
- s40 leaves out CDC's "person or animal".
- s62 says "plague areas" where CDC says "endemic areas".
- There's no general disclaimer line in the narration.

issues.claim: CDC describes one moment on a trail when the risk quietly goes up. It's not when you see an animal. It's when the animals vanish.
issues.problem: CDC talks about places where rodents have recently died from plague. 'Animals vanish' is our paraphrase, not CDC's description, and burrows can be empty for harmless reasons. The open loop is fine, but crediting the exact framing to CDC overstates what the page says.
issues.fix: And stick around, because CDC warns about one situation outdoors where the risk goes up. It's not when you see an animal. It's when the animals have suddenly died off.

issues.claim: So a prairie dog town that's suddenly silent, with empty burrows where animals used to be? That's your cue to keep your distance.
issues.problem: This is a reasonable inference from CDC's die-off warning, but it should be tied to signs of a die-off rather than silence alone.
issues.fix: So a prairie dog town that's suddenly gone quiet, especially with dead animals around? That's your cue to keep your distance, and to report dead animals to your local health department.

issues.claim: that kind of spread requires direct and close contact with the person who has pneumonic plague
issues.problem: CDC's wording is 'the person or animal with pneumonic plague'. The animal part matters because the video covers sick cats.
issues.fix: And CDC says that kind of spread requires direct and close contact with the person or animal with pneumonic plague.

issues.claim: dogs or cats that roam free in plague areas
issues.problem: CDC's wording is 'endemic areas'. The meaning is the same, so this is optional precision.
issues.fix: Third, the bed. CDC advises not letting dogs or cats that roam free in areas where plague occurs sleep on your bed.

issues.claim: If you're worried, talk to a health professional.
issues.problem: The safety line is there, but no general disclaimer is spoken or shown.
issues.fix: Narration: "This video is for general education, not medical advice. If you're worried, talk to a health professional." On-screen: "Education, not medical advice. Worried? Talk to a professional"

audio.soundNotes: Music sits right in the -12/-15 target (measured -13.5 under voice, -13.2 in pauses) so a small -0.5dB trim (0.95x) keeps it from creeping to the loud edge while staying felt. The stock cue auto-leveler did most of the work, but a cluster of pops/blips/swooshes land 6-13dB hotter than the -14/-20 speech target (e.g. during the fast chip/stat bursts) and a few whoosh/pop pairs in pauses (LA 1924 reveal, 'curable' and the pet-roaming beat) sit at -3 to -5dB, almost voice level — I pulled those down and dropped the most redundant simultaneous layer (tick/pop stacked with swoosh at the same timestamp) rather than cutting everything, to avoid thinning out real transitions. Dramatic/serious beats (animals vanish, hands off, call urgently) get a bespoke subtle SFX instead of stock pops so they don't feel cartoonish next to a sober line.

issues: Worried-face mascot adds mild tension but stays within guardrails (no horror framing)
Subhead 'PETS, HIKES, CAMPING' is small but readable at phone size
Backpack icon has no clear visual link to 'plague cases' or fleas, so the focal point is confusing rather than curiosity-building
No face/emotion on the mascot, lower emotional pull than the other two
Red arrow pointing at an unrelated object adds clutter without payoff
Calm reassurance is accurate and on-brand but has a smaller curiosity gap than #0's open question

thumbnail.reasoning: All three are legible at phone size with clean 2-line headlines, safe-frame text, brand-colored backgrounds, and no graphic/doom imagery. #1 ('5 A Year') uses the proven number-pattern headline, but its backpack mascot is a mismatched, faceless focal point that doesn't visually connect to plague cases or fleas — it adds clutter rather than curiosity and loses emotional pull. #2 ('Rare. Treatable.') is calm, accurate, and matches the channel's successful calm-framing approach, but it answers a 'is it dangerous' question rather than the title's 'where it occurs / how to stay safe' promise, giving it a smaller curiosity gap. #0 ('It's the Fleas') best fits the title: it opens a genuine curiosity gap (what's the main route), ties directly to practical prevention (pets, hikes, camping) which speaks to the audience, uses a single clear mascot focal point with a hint of relatable tension (not fear-mongering), and pays off exactly what the video promises. It has the strongest combination of curiosity + relevance + legibility without overclaiming.
